\documentclass[11pt]{article}
\usepackage[margin=1in]{geometry}

\title{Formative Assessment in Rural Primary Schools:
A Pilot Study in the Northern Districts}
\author{L. Mbeki and T. Agyeman}
\date{April 2026}

\begin{document}
\maketitle

\begin{abstract}
This report summarises a pilot study of formative assessment
in rural primary schools.
Forty teachers was trained in the use of short diagnostic
quizzes.
The project lost it's funding after the first year, yet most
schools continued the practice.
Participants gave a honest account of the difficulties they
faced.
However, the curriculum do not address the needs of pupils
who miss school during the harvest season.
\end{abstract}

\section{Introduction}
Formative assessment, the practice of checking pupil
understanding during rather than after a unit of study, has
been promoted in the district's teacher colleges for a
decade.
Adoption in rural schools has lagged behind the towns, and
the reasons are not well understood.
The pilot study reported here placed short diagnostic
quizzes in forty rural classrooms and followed their use
over two school years.
This report describes the design of the pilot, the pattern
of uptake, and the obstacles teachers reported.

\section{Study Design}
Forty primary schools were selected from the northern
districts in consultation with the district education
office.
Half received a term of weekly coaching visits, while the
remainder received printed materials only.
Teachers kept a log of each quiz administered, and project
staff observed one lesson per term in every school.
The comparison between coached and uncoached schools is
reported separately; the present volume concerns the
qualitative findings that emerged across both arms.

\section{Obstacles Reported by Teachers}
Teachers welcomed the quizzes but reported three recurring
obstacles.
Large class sizes made individual feedback difficult, and
many teachers preferred to use the quizzes with the whole
class at once.
Irregular attendance during the harvest season disrupted
the sequence of units on which the quizzes were mapped.
Finally, several schools lacked a reliable stock of paper,
and teachers copied quiz questions onto the blackboard at
the cost of lesson time.

\section{Outlook}
A follow-up study with a larger sample is planned for the
coming school year, and the district office has signalled
interest in aligning the quiz bank with the revised
syllabus.
\end{document}
